'''II.''' ''n.'' A medicine for relieving coughs; a pectoral.

''bêche''), a spade; Pr. ''beca'', a hook, Ir. ''bacc'', a hook.] An agricultural implement with two hooks, used in dressing turnips, etc.; a form of mattock.

'''beck<sup>4</sup>†''' (bek), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bek'', ''bec'', < OF. ''bec'', beak; the same word, retaining the orig. short vowel, as the now more common ''beak''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A beak.—'''2.''' Any pointed or projecting part of the dress, especially of a head-dress, as of the bycocket.

'''beck<sup>5</sup>''' (bek), ''n.'' [Prob. another form of ''back''<sup>3</sup>, q. v.] A vat or vessel used in a dye-house; a back.—{{smaller|'''Clearing-beck''', in ''calico-printing'', a vat in which cottons printed with certain colors are cleansed or scoured with soap and water.}}

'''beck<sup>6</sup>†''', ''n.'' [Cf. ''beak''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''beck-harman''.

'''becker''' (bek′ėr), ''n.'' [E. dial. (also ''becket''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.), appar. < ''beck''<sup>4</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. F. ''beccard'', the female salmon.] A name of the fish ''Sparus pagrus'', otherwise called ''braize'' and ''king of the sea-breams''.

'''beckern''' (bek′ėrn), ''n.'' Same as ''bickern'' and ''beak-iron''.

'''becket<sup>1</sup>''' (bek′et), ''n.'' [E. dial.; cf. OF. ''bequet'', ''bechet'', a pike or pickerel, dim. of ''bec'', beak: see ''beak''<sup>1</sup>, ''beck''<sup>4</sup>.] Same as ''becker''.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''becket<sup>2</sup>''' (bek′et), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] ''Naut.'': (''a'') A short piece of rope, with a knot at one
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Beckets.}}}}
end and an eye in the other, for temporarily confining ropes or small spars. (''b'') A handle made of a rope grommet or ring. (''c'') A wooden cleat or hook, fastened on the fore- or main-rigging of a ship, for the tacks and sheets to lie in when not in use. (''d'') A rope grommet in the bottom of a block for securing the standing end of the fall. (''e'') A cant term for a trousers-pocket.

'''becket<sup>2</sup>''' (bek′et), ''v. t.'' [< ''becket<sup>2</sup>'', ''n.''] To fasten or provide with beckets. ''Cooper.''

'''beck-harman†''', ''n.'' [Also ''harman-beck;'' old slang, of obscure origin; with ''beck'' cf. equiv. ''beak<sup>2</sup>''.] In old slang, a constable. ''B. Jonson.''

'''becking†''' (bek′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''beck<sup>2</sup>'', ''v.''] The act of making a beck; the act of bowing or nodding.
{{smaller block|The Communion was altogether like a popish mass, with the old apish tricks of Antichrist, bowings and ''beckings'', kneelings and knockings, the Lord’s Death, after St. Paul’s doctrine, neither preached nor spoken of.
{{right|''Bp. Bale'', in R. W. Dixon’s Hist. Ch. of Eng., xxi.}}}}

'''bec-de-corbin†''' (bek′dė-kôr-baṅ′), ''n.''   [F., lit. crow’s beak: see ''beak''<sup>1</sup>, ''de''<sup>2</sup>, and ''corbie.'']   '''1.''' A name given {{img float|file=century v01 p0523 c1f1.png|width=233px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Becs-de-corbin, 15th century.}} {{smaller|''A'', with handle of wrought-iron; ''B'', with wooden handle sheathed with metal. (From Viollet-le-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}} in the middle ages to the pointed end of the martel-de-fer, or war-hammer. Hence—'''2.''' The whole weapon having such a point or beak. —'''3.''' A name given in the eighteenth century to the head of a walking-cane having somewhat the form of a bird’s beak.

'''bechamel''' (besh′ạ-mel), ''n.''   [< F. ''béchamel'': see definition.]   In ''cookery'', a white sauce of elaborate composition, named from its inventor, Louis de Béchamel or Béchameil, marquis of Nointel, steward to Louis XIV.

'''bechance'''<sup>1</sup> (bē-chȧns′), ''v.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''chance'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To happen; chance.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To befall; happen to.
{{smaller block|My sons — God knows what hath ''bechanced'' them.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 4.}}}}

'''bechance'''<sup>2</sup>† (bē-chȧns′), ''adv.''   [For ''by chance''; cf. ''because.'']   Accidentally; by chance.
{{smaller block|We ''bechance'' lost our sovereign lord.
{{right|''Grafton'', Hen. VIII., an. 14.}}}}

{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Prithee, interrupt not
The paradise of my ''becharming'' thoughts.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Fancies, iv. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A medicine for relieving coughs; a pectoral.

''bæk''; but the ME. form may be from the Scand., the only authenticated AS. form being ''bece'', ''bæce'', dat. of ''bece'' (giving mod. E. *''betch'', which prob. exists in the dial. ''batch'': see ''batch''<sup>2</sup>) = OS. ''beki'' = OD. ''beke'', D. ''beek'' = LG. ''beke'', ''bäk'' = OHG. ''bah'', MHG. ''bach'', a brook.]   '''1.''' A brook; a small stream; especially, a brook with a stony bed or rugged course.
{{smaller block|The brooks, the ''becks'', the rills.

'''2.''' The valley of a beck; a field or patch of ground adjacent to a brook. See ''batch''<sup>2</sup>.

32

{{smaller block|<poem>Who ’s he but bowed if this great prince but ''becked''?</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Queen Margaret.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let us follow
The ''becking'' of our chance.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Two Noble Kinsmen, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' To recognize a person by a slight bow or nod. [Scotch.]

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To summon or intimate some command or desire to by a nod or gesture; beckon to.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bell, book, and candle shall not drive me back,
When gold and silver ''becks'' me to come on.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To express by a gesture: as, to ''beck'' thanks. [Rare.]

'''beck'''<sup>2</sup> (bek), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bek'', < ''beken'', ''becken'', beck: see ''beck''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A nod of the head or other significant gesture intended to be understood as expressive of a desire, or as a sign of command.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nods, and ''becks'', and wreathed smiles.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', L’Allegro, l. 28.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My guiltiness had need of such a master,
That with a ''beck'' can suppress multitudes.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', The Witch, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|I would wish myself a little more command and sovereignty; that all the court were subject to my absolute ''beck''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' A gesture of salutation or recognition; a bow; a courtesy. [Scotch.]—'''At one’s beck, at one’s beck and call''', {{smaller|subject to one’s slightest wish; obliged or ready to obey all of one’s orders or desires.}}
{{smaller block|It was necessary for him to have always ''at his beck'' some men of letters from Paris to point out the solecisms and false rhymes of which, to the last, he was frequently guilty. {{right|''Macaulay'', Frederic the Great.}}}}
<poem>We move, my friend,
''At no man’s beck.'' {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iii.}}</poem>

'''beck<sup>3</sup>''' (bek), ''n.''   [E. dial., not found in ME., < AS. ''becca'', glossed ''ligo'', a mattock; cf. ML. ''becca'' (cf. ML. ''besca'', > OF. ''besche'', mod. F. ''bêche''), a spade; Pr. ''beca'', a hook, Ir. ''bacc'', a hook.]   An agricultural implement with two hooks, used in dressing turnips, etc.; a form of mattock.

'''beck<sup>4</sup>†''' (bek), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bek'', ''bec'', < OF. ''bec'', beak; the same word, retaining the orig. short vowel, as the now more common ''beak''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A beak.—'''2.''' Any pointed or projecting part of the dress, especially of a head-dress, as of the bycocket.

'''beck<sup>5</sup>''' (bek), ''n.''   [Prob. another form of ''back''<sup>3</sup>, q. v.]   A vat or vessel used in a dye-house; a back.—{{smaller|'''Clearing-beck''', in ''calico-printing'', a vat in which cottons printed with certain colors are cleansed or scoured with soap and water.}}

'''beck<sup>6</sup>†''', ''n.''   [Cf. ''beak''<sup>2</sup>.]   Same as ''beck-harman''.

'''becker''' (bek′ėr), ''n.''   [E. dial. (also ''becket''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.), appar. < ''beck''<sup>4</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. F. ''beccard'', the female salmon.]   A name of the fish ''Sparus pagrus'', otherwise called ''braize'' and ''king of the sea-breams''.

'''beckern''' (bek′ėrn), ''n.'' Same as ''bickern'' and ''beak-iron''.

'''becket<sup>1</sup>''' (bek′et), ''n.''   [E. dial.; cf. OF. ''bequet'', ''bechet'', a pike or pickerel, dim. of ''bec'', beak: see ''beak''<sup>1</sup>, ''beck''<sup>4</sup>.]   Same as ''becker''.

'''becket<sup>2</sup>''' (bek′et), ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   ''Naut.'': (''a'') A short piece of rope, with a knot at one {{img float|file=century v01 p0523 c2f1.png|width=229px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Beckets.}}}} end and an eye in the other, for temporarily confining ropes or small spars. (''b'') A handle made of a rope grommet or ring. (''c'') A wooden cleat or hook, fastened on the fore- or main-rigging of a ship, for the tacks and sheets to lie in when not in use. (''d'') A rope grommet in the bottom of a block for securing the standing end of the fall. (''e'') A cant term for a trousers-pocket.

'''becket<sup>2</sup>''' (bek′et), ''v. t.''   [< ''becket<sup>2</sup>'', ''n.'']   To fasten or provide with beckets.   ''Cooper.''

'''beck-harman†''', ''n.''   [Also ''harman-beck;'' old slang, of obscure origin; with ''beck'' cf. equiv. ''beak<sup>2</sup>''.]   In old slang, a constable.   ''B. Jonson.''

'''becking†''' (bek′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''beck<sup>2</sup>'', ''v.'']   The act of making a beck; the act of bowing or nodding.
{{smaller block|The Communion was altogether like a popish mass, with the old apish tricks of Antichrist, bowings and ''beckings'', kneelings and knockings, the Lord’s Death, after St. Paul’s doctrine, neither preached nor spoken of.
{{right|''Bp. Bale'', in R. W. Dixon’s Hist. Ch. of Eng., xxi.}}}}

'''beck-iron''' (bek′ī″ėrn), ''n.''   [< ''beck''<sup>4</sup> + ''iron.'' Cf. ''beak-iron.'']   '''1.''' A contrivance for holding a piece of wood firmly while it is planed. {{smaller|It is made of iron or steel rods fastened to a bench and bent parallel to the surface of the wood.}}

'''2.''' A small anvil with a shallow groove, for rounding the inside of the bows of scissors.

'''beckon''' (bek′n), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. also ''becken,'' < ME. ''beknen, becnen, beknien,'' < AS. ''bēcnian, biécnan,'' later also ''beácnian'' (OS. ''bōknian'' = OHG. ''bouhnen'' = ON. ''bākna''), < ''beácen,'' a sign, beacon: see ''beacon.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To make a significant gesture with the head or hand, intended as a hint or an intimation, especially of a desire for approach or departure, or for silence.
{{smaller block|Alexander ''beckoned'' with the hand, and would have made his defence unto the people. {{right|Acts xix. 33.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make a significant sign to; summon or direct by making signs.
{{smaller block|<poem>I see a hand you cannot see,
Which ''beckons'' me away.</poem>
{{right|''Tickell'', Colin and Lucy.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Beckoning'' the imagination with promises better than any fulfilment. {{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 325.}}}}

'''beckon''' (bek′n), ''n.''   [< ''beckon, v.'']   A significant gesture: as, “at the first ''beckon,''” ''Bolingbroke'', Parties. [Rare.]

'''beckoner''' (bek′n-ėr), ''n.'' One who beckons or calls by signs.

'''beclap†''' (bē-klap′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beclappen''; ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''clap''<sup>1</sup>.]   To catch; grasp; insnare.
{{smaller block|<poem>He that with his thousand cordes slye
Continuelly us waiteth to ''biclappe.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Second Nun’s Tale, l. 9.}}}}

'''beclip†''' (bē-klip′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beclippen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''clip''<sup>1</sup>.]   To embrace; clasp.
{{smaller block|<poem>And sodenly, ere she it wiste,
''Beclipt'' in armes he her kiste.</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i.}}}}

'''becloud''' (bē-kloud′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''cloud.'']   To overcloud; obscure; dim.
{{smaller block|Storms of tears ''becloud'' his eyes.
{{right|''P. Fletcher'', Piscatory Eclogues, v. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|The subject has been ''beclouded'' by the mass of writings.
{{right|''The American'', VIII. 60.}}}}

'''become''' (bē-kum′), ''v.''; pret. ''became'', pp. ''become'', ppr. ''becoming''.   [Early mod. E. also ''becum'', ''becume'', < ME. ''becumen'', ''bicumen'', < AS. ''becuman'', ''bicuman'', come, happen (= D. ''bekomen'' = OHG. ''biqueman'', MHG. ''bekomen'', G. ''bekommen'', reach, suit, = Goth. ''bikwiman'', come upon one, befall), < ''be-'' + ''cuman'', come: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''come.'' In the sense of befit, suit, cf. AS. ''gecwēme'', ME. ''icweme'', ''cweme'', and OHG. ''biquāmi'', MHG. ''bequæme'', G. ''bequem'', fit, suitable; also AS. ''cymlīc'', E. ''comely'', and L. ''convenien(t-)s'', E. ''convenient.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To come; arrive; betake one’s self; go.
{{smaller block|But when they saw that they shoulde ''become'' vnder the obedience of another prince, they suffred the Greekes to meet Alexander.
{{right|''J. Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|You shall have sometimes fair houses so full of glass that one cannot tell where to ''become'' to be out of the sun or cold. {{right|''Bacon'', Building.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I cannot joy, until I be resolv’d
Where our right valiant father is ''become''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' To come about; come into being; pass from non-existence; arise. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The only reals for him [Hume] were certain irrelated sensations, and out of these knowledge arises or ''becomes.''
{{right|''Mind'', XI. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' To change or pass from one state of existence to another; come to be something different; come or grow to be: as, the boy rapidly ''becomes'' the man.
{{smaller block|The Lord God . . . breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man ''became'' a living soul.
{{right|Gen. ii. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I rue
That errour now, which is ''become'' my crime.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 1181.}}}}
{{smaller block|If the Bank be unconstitutional, when did it ''become'' so?
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Sept. 30, 1834.}}}}
'''4.''' To be fit or proper; be decorous or praiseworthy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Set this diamond safe
In golden palaces, as it ''becomes.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3.}}}}

'''To become of.''' {{smaller|(''a''†) To come out of; result from. See 1. (''b'') To be the fate of; be the end of; be the final or subsequent condition: after ''what:'' as, ''what'' will ''become of'' our commerce? ''what'' will ''become of'' us? It applies to place as well as condition: ''What'' has ''become of'' my friend? that is, where is he? as well as, what is his condition?}}
{{smaller block|''What'' is then ''become of'' so huge a multitude? ''Raleigh.''
<poem>''Sneer.'' And pray ''what becomes of'' her?
''Puff.'' She is gone to throw herself into the sea, to be sure.</poem>
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Critic, iii. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To suit or be suitable to; be congruous with; befit; accord with in charac-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
